description: We are FUERZA G, a multidisciplinary team comprising a Systems Engineering student, an Environmental Engineering graduate, a Business Administration and Marketing graduate, and a Science and Technology Education student. We met at Universidad Continental and are united by curiosity, collaboration, and a commitment to continuous learning. By combining our perspectives, we turn ideas into purposeful proposals and tackle new challenges together.
summary: Children are curious about space: what lies beyond Earth and what humans have left behind. 1202 ALARM is a 3D educational game driven by a storyline, designed for young people aged 9 to 14. It can be played through a web browser on both computers and mobile phones, turning that curiosity into an interactive gaming experience. Players guide Kuri, an astronaut guinea pig, through seven missions: three on the Moon (Apollo 11, 12, and 15) and four on Mars (Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit and Opportunity, and InSight). In each mission, Kuri lands at the actual location, explores the surroundings, and reactivates a NASA machine that has been left inactive. Along the way, players discover why it was sent there, what it accomplished, what challenges it faced, and how it eventually ended up abandoned at that location. The name comes from the 1202 alarm that sounded during the Apollo 11 lunar landing, when Mission Control decided to continue with the mission. Here, every mistake is an opportunity to learn. Although the story is fictional, the science is real and based on data from the NSSDCA and NASA Science. Whenever information about a particular detail is unavailable, the game marks it as "to be verified" rather than making assumptions. Available in Spanish, English, and Portuguese.
details:
What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

1202 Alarm is a 3D exploration and survival video game that runs directly in a web browser, with no installation required. Its story is fictional, but it is based on real NASA records. The story takes place in the near future, when NASA is shutting down its operations. In this context, Director Harrison orders one final mission: to recover the machines the agency left behind in space.

To carry out this mission, two fictional astronauts, Lucy Ramos and Matt Quispe, secretly bring Kuri, a guinea pig that had been trained in laboratories years earlier. They hide him inside a sample container. During the journey, an electrical failure interrupts radio communications and leaves the Kuntur lander without fuel, meaning it can now carry only 2 kg. In addition, one of the astronauts is ill, so the crew must remain aboard the Wayra spacecraft to keep the life-support systems running. For this reason, Kuri is the only one who can descend to the surface.

From the spacecraft, Lucy, a voice from Mission Control, guides Kuri over the radio and shares interesting facts to help him complete his mission. However, Kuri must figure out on his own how each machine works and what he needs to do to accomplish his mission. The game begins with an 85-second introduction in an illustrated comic-book format. During this section, players also learn the controls through Kuri's training. As the game progresses, the story continues through comic-book scenes that appear as introductory sequences between different parts of the gameplay. Another special feature of this interactive game is Kuri's portable greenhouse, where he can grow his own food and take care of his crops.

The seven missions follow four stages:

1. Landing: Kuri must control his descent using the available fuel. To do so, he needs to monitor his vertical speed, horizontal speed, altitude, and landing zone. Each mission is based on the actual conditions of the corresponding space missions. For example, Apollo 12 landed approximately 180 meters from Surveyor 3, so its landing zone is small. In the case of Viking, the initially planned landing site was too rough, so the player must find a safer area.

2. Exploration: Kuri explores different locations on the Moon or Mars in 3D. To find his way, he has a flashlight attached to his helmet, a map, and indicators showing his oxygen level, suit battery, and health. Along the way, he discovers points of interest that require different actions, such as locating a machine, digging with a robotic arm, collecting air sample bags, scanning objects, pointing an antenna toward Earth, connecting the six instruments at the Apollo 12 station, or making decisions about the use of certain equipment, such as the television camera.

3. What Went Wrong: Kuri investigates the problems each machine experienced and must arrange the events in the order in which they actually happened.

4. The Machine's Case File: Using the clues he has collected, Kuri answers questions about the machine's location, purpose, achievements, how its mission ended, and its current status. If he answers correctly, he manages to "reconnect" it. The machine then plays its final message and gives him a knot from a quipu, which will be used to transmit the signal back to Earth.

Between missions, Kuri returns to Kuntur Station. This base has rooms where recovered objects are stored, a control center with a clue archive, and a hologram of the current mission. It also has a greenhouse where Kuri can grow Andean crops such as potatoes, corn, lettuce, and quinoa. Progress is saved automatically. Players can also earn badges by completing missions without mistakes, collecting 25 clues, or harvesting their crops.

The video game is available in Spanish, English, and Portuguese. It can be played using a keyboard or touchscreen controls, and players can adjust the volume of the music, sound effects, and voices separately.

Benefits

The main benefit is that children learn while playing. Instead of presenting all the information through lengthy texts, the game allows them to discover facts through actions, clues, and questions. It also aims to make scientific information easier to remember.

For example, the game presents real facts such as the Apollo 11 descent engine's operating time, which was 756.3 seconds, and the time the lunar module reached the surface: 20:17:40 UT. Another example is the Opportunity rover, which traveled 45.16 km before losing communication due to a global dust storm on June 10, 2018. The game also introduces InSight, whose robotic arm, measuring more than 1.8 meters in length, was used to place a seismometer on the surface of Mars.

If players answer incorrectly, they do not lose the game. Instead, they can review the clues and try again, encouraging them to learn from their mistakes. Furthermore, since the game runs directly in a browser, it requires no installation and can be played on both computers and mobile phones. It is also available in three languages.

Expected Impact

With this project, we want children to see these machines as more than just old equipment abandoned in space. We want them to understand that they were part of important exploration missions, that each had a purpose, and that even though they stopped communicating, their discoveries remain important.

By recovering the "voices" of each machine, players learn what NASA sent into space, what it discovered, and how each mission came to an end. In this way, we hope to spark their interest in space exploration and encourage them to keep learning about the universe.

All the scientific information used in the game comes from NASA sources and is clearly identified as real. Meanwhile, the events and characters in the story are explicitly presented as fictional. At the end of the game, a screen appears with the question "Will this story continue?", introducing the Kepler Space Telescope as the next destination. This leaves open the possibility of continuing the project by exploring new worlds and space missions.

Tools and Technology

The video game is developed in a single HTML file and uses JavaScript to run. Three.js, an open-source library, was used to create the 3D environments and elements. The game also uses the browser's audio and local storage features to play sounds and automatically save progress.

The game is hosted on Netlify and works in any modern web browser.

During development, we used Claude as a programming assistant to write and correct the code. We also used ChatGPT and Gemini to create and improve images and visual design elements.

To develop the scientific content, we consulted official NASA sources, including NSSDCA spacecraft records for the Apollo 11, Apollo 12, and Apollo 15 missions, as well as NASA Science pages about Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder, the Mars Exploration Rovers, and InSight. All times displayed in the game are expressed in UT (Universal Time), following the format used by the NSSDCA.

What Makes Our Project Creative?

One of the most distinctive elements of the video game is its main character: Kuri, an astronaut guinea pig. We chose this animal because of its important place in Andean culture, allowing us to incorporate elements of our identity into the context of space exploration.

This theme is also reflected in other elements of the story: the Wayra spacecraft, whose name means "wind"; the Kuntur lander, whose name means "condor"; the quipu, used to transmit the signal back to Earth; and the greenhouse where Andean crops are grown.

Another distinctive feature is that each machine has a final message that players can recover. In this way, reactivating a machine is not simply about completing a task, but also about discovering its history and what it accomplished during its mission.

The project's name, 1202 ALARM, refers to a real alarm that nearly interrupted the first Moon landing. We also want the game to provide reliable information. Whenever we cannot find a particular fact in NASA sources, we mark it as "pending verification" rather than making up an answer.

Factors We Considered as a Team

  • Accuracy: Although the story is fictional, we use real NASA information to represent the machines, dates, coordinates, and mission results. We make sure to distinguish real facts from elements created for the story.
  • Age (9 to 14 years): We adapt the questions to include three answer choices. We also provide clues that allow players to review the information when they make a mistake. The video game contains no violent scenes.
  • Accessibility: The game works on computers and mobile phones, is available in three languages, and has separate volume controls. Players can also skip cinematic scenes.
  • Respect: The astronauts and the director are fictional characters. This allows us to avoid portraying real people as part of the story.
  • Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence: We use artificial intelligence tools to support programming and visual design. However, the decisions regarding the story and scientific content were made by our team and cross-checked against official NASA sources.
